## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with depression on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and support from prior literature. Across the full set of results, immune and inflammatory signaling emerges as the most prominent theme. The strongest signal is cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, P < 3.97 × 10−19, 34 associated proteins), followed by tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (Reactome:R-HSA-5669034, P < 5.76 × 10−11, 11 associated proteins) and Cytokines and inflammatory response (WikiPathways:530, P < 1.81 × 10−4, 6 associated proteins). This pattern is highly consistent with a large body of literature showing that elevated inflammatory cytokine signaling, including tumor necrosis factor and interleukin pathways, may contribute to depressive symptoms through effects on monoamine metabolism, synaptic plasticity, neuroendocrine function, and microglial activation. In the same general direction, the enrichment of interferon regulatory factor motif targets (Transcription factor:M08887_1, P < 4.06 × 10−2, 7 associated proteins) further supports the possible involvement of innate immune transcriptional programs, which have repeatedly been linked to inflammation-associated depression.

Building on this immune-centered pattern, the enrichment results also suggest involvement of transcriptional stress-response pathways. In particular, p53 motif targets (Transcription factor:M10023_1, P < 1.10 × 10−2, 17 associated proteins) were enriched. p53 is widely implicated in cellular stress, apoptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction, and previous studies suggest that excessive p53-related signaling may contribute to neuronal loss, impaired neurogenesis, and stress susceptibility in depressive disorders. In parallel, receptor complex (Gene Ontology:0043235, P < 2.04 × 10−9, 24 associated proteins) highlights altered receptor-mediated signaling, which is relevant because depression has been associated with dysregulation of cytokine receptors, neurotransmitter receptors, and neurotrophic signaling complexes.

A related layer of the enrichment profile points toward altered secretory and trafficking biology. This pattern includes post-translational protein phosphorylation (Reactome:R-HSA-8957275, P < 5.35 × 10−5, 11 associated proteins), cargo receptor activity (Gene Ontology:0038024, P < 2.77 × 10−5, 8 associated proteins), endoplasmic reticulum lumen (Gene Ontology:0005788, P < 1.67 × 10−6, 17 associated proteins), and lipid localization (Gene Ontology:0010876, P < 1.65 × 10−4, 15 associated proteins). These findings are biologically plausible because endoplasmic reticulum stress, abnormal protein processing, membrane lipid imbalance, and defective vesicular transport have all been reported in depression and may influence synaptic receptor trafficking, inflammatory mediator secretion, and neuronal resilience. Along the same lines, the enrichment of carbohydrate binding (Gene Ontology:0030246, P < 4.83 × 10−6, 11 associated proteins) may also reflect altered lectin-like, extracellular matrix, or immune recognition processes, which have been implicated in neuroimmune communication.

Extending beyond canonical neuronal and immune pathways, the enrichment profile also includes tissue- and host-interaction-related signals. These include symbiont entry into host cell (Gene Ontology:0046718, P < 5.11 × 10−8, 11 associated proteins), Colon; goblet cells [Human Protein Atlas:0130892, P < 4.69 × 10−8, 23 associated proteins], and Colon; endocrine cells [Human Protein Atlas:0131293, P < 2.62 × 10−6, 17 associated proteins]. Although these are not classic psychiatric pathways, they may be compatible with growing evidence for gut-immune-brain interactions in depression. Goblet cells regulate mucosal barrier integrity, while enteroendocrine cells influence serotonin production, immune tone, and vagal signaling; disturbances in these systems have been associated with depressive phenotypes in both clinical and preclinical studies. Finally, the overlap with inflammatory disease pathways such as Rheumatoid arthritis (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:05323, P < 3.38 × 10−6, 11 associated proteins) further supports the concept that depression may share molecular mechanisms with systemic inflammatory disorders, consistent with the well-documented comorbidity between chronic inflammation and depressive illness. Overall, these results suggest that depression in this dataset is strongly linked to convergent mechanisms involving immune activation, stress-responsive transcription, receptor signaling, and secretory and gut-associated biology.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Factor: IRF; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (TF:M08887_1) 

Interferon regulatory factor represents a family of sequence-specific transcriptional regulators that bind deoxyribonucleic acid motifs enriched in guanine and adenine residues, including the consensus-like element described here. These regulators are central components of innate and adaptive immune signaling. They are activated downstream of pattern-recognition receptors, cytokine receptors, and nucleic acid sensing pathways, and they control transcriptional programs involved in type one interferon production, antiviral defense, antigen presentation, inflammatory cytokine release, microglial activation, and immune cell differentiation. In the central nervous system, interferon regulatory factor activity can influence neuroimmune communication by altering the expression of inflammatory mediators in microglia, astrocytes, endothelial cells, and infiltrating immune cells. Because depression is increasingly understood to involve immune dysregulation, chronic low-grade inflammation, stress-induced changes in cytokine signaling, and altered neuroplasticity, transcriptional programs governed by interferon regulatory factor proteins are biologically plausible contributors to disease mechanisms. More specifically, sustained activation of interferon-related transcription can promote inflammatory signaling, disturb monoamine metabolism through induction of enzymes in the tryptophan degradation pathway, impair synaptic plasticity, and alter hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, all of which have been implicated in depressive symptom development.

Building on this biological background, the relevance of this motif-defined pathway to depression can be considered in a cautious mechanistic framework.

No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a direct literature-grounded pathway-to-disease synthesis specific to this pathway cannot be supported with the requested citation evidence. Nevertheless, from a mechanistic perspective, a pathway defined by interferon regulatory factor binding motifs is plausibly related to depression because interferon regulatory factor proteins are major transcriptional mediators of innate immune activation, and immune activation is a well-established biological dimension of depressive illness. When these transcription factors are activated, they can increase expression of type one interferons and other inflammatory mediators, which may amplify neuroinflammation, influence microglial reactivity, reduce neurotrophic support, and shift tryptophan metabolism away from serotonin synthesis toward potentially neuroactive catabolites. Such changes provide a biologically coherent route through which interferon regulatory factor dependent transcription could contribute to anhedonia, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and mood disturbance. However, because the publication list supplied here is empty, any stronger claim about the specific role of this motif-defined pathway in depression would be inferential rather than evidence-based within the constraints of the provided materials.

In parallel with this cautious interpretation, the enrichment results provide a quantitative indication that this pathway captures a broad set of depression-associated proteins.

There were 127 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the interferon regulatory factor family of sequence-specific transcriptional regulators, indicating a quantitatively substantial convergence of disease-linked proteins on immune transcriptional control, inflammatory signaling, antiviral defense, antigen presentation, cytokine release, microglial activation, and immune cell differentiation. This protein count of 127 supports the interpretation that interferon regulatory factor-governed biology is not represented by an isolated signal, but rather by a broad and coordinated functional module that is highly relevant to depression, particularly in the context of chronic low-grade inflammation, stress-related cytokine dysregulation, altered neuroimmune communication, disturbed tryptophan metabolism, impaired synaptic plasticity, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis disruption, all of which have been repeatedly implicated in depressive symptom development. In the central nervous system, the enrichment pattern is biologically plausible because transcriptional programs downstream of interferon regulatory factor proteins can influence multiple cell populations simultaneously, including microglia, astrocytes, endothelial cells, and infiltrating immune cells, thereby amplifying inflammatory mediator production across several interacting compartments rather than within a single isolated cell type.

To complement this enrichment summary, the network view below illustrates how these 127 proteins are connected at the level of protein-protein interaction.

Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 127 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and further exploration.

Following this network-level overview, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several individual proteins that may be especially informative for interpreting the pathway in relation to depression.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling proteins in this list in relation to depression because it sits at the interface between peripheral innate immunity, microbial sensing, and inflammatory cytokine production. A substantial body of depression research implicates chronic low-grade inflammation, exaggerated cytokine signaling, and gut microbiota-derived immune activation in the pathophysiology of depressive disorders. By facilitating lipopolysaccharide and toll-like receptor 4 signaling and downstream nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation, CD14 may contribute to the systemic inflammatory tone that is frequently observed in major depressive disorder, particularly in patients with elevated C-reactive protein or treatment-resistant illness. Its additional role in recognizing microbial lipoproteins supports a plausible link to gut barrier dysfunction and endotoxemia, both of which have been proposed to drive neuroimmune activation, sickness behavior, and anhedonia. Therefore, CD14 is highly relevant as a mechanistic bridge between peripheral immune challenge and central mood dysregulation.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending this immune-centered perspective, the next protein points toward inflammatory remodeling and stress-responsive myeloid biology.

CHI3L1 is notable because it integrates inflammation, tissue remodeling, and myeloid-cell polarization, all of which are increasingly implicated in depression. Depression is now understood in many patients as a disorder with a strong immunometabolic and neuroinflammatory component, involving altered macrophage activation, cytokine production, and stress-induced tissue responses. CHI3L1 promotes inflammatory signaling, including AKT1-dependent interleukin 8 production, and influences dendritic cell and macrophage behavior, suggesting a role in shaping peripheral and possibly central immune states relevant to depressive symptomatology. Its broader function in helping cells cope with environmental stress further aligns with models in which chronic stress induces maladaptive immune and epithelial responses that feed into mood dysregulation. For these reasons, CHI3L1 stands out as a plausible marker and mediator of the inflammatory-biological subtype of depression.

A related but distinct aspect of immune imbalance is reflected by proteins that regulate lymphocyte survival and differentiation.

LGALS1 is relevant to depression because it is a potent immunoregulatory lectin with direct effects on T-cell survival and differentiation. Immune dysregulation in depression involves not only elevated inflammatory mediators but also altered adaptive immune balance, including abnormalities in T-cell subsets and immune exhaustion-like states. LGALS1 can induce T-cell apoptosis and modulate T helper 17 biology, which is noteworthy because T helper 17-associated cytokines and broader T-cell imbalance have been linked to depressive symptoms, neuroinflammation, and stress vulnerability. In addition, galectins can affect cell-cell communication and inflammatory resolution, raising the possibility that LGALS1 participates in the transition between acute stress responses and chronic maladaptive inflammation. Thus, LGALS1 may be important in depression through its capacity to reshape immune homeostasis rather than simply amplify inflammation.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

This theme of immune regulation is further refined by proteins that may buffer excessive cytokine signaling.

IL18BP is of particular interest because it counter-regulates interleukin 18, a cytokine repeatedly implicated in stress-related inflammation and depressive phenotypes. Elevated interleukin 18 signaling has been associated with inflammasome activation, neuroimmune stress responses, and behavioral changes resembling sickness and depression. As a natural inhibitor of interleukin 18, IL18BP may reflect an endogenous buffering mechanism against excessive T helper 1-skewed inflammation. In the context of depression, altered IL18BP levels could indicate failed compensation for inflammatory activation or identify patients in whom inflammasome-associated pathways are especially relevant. This makes IL18BP potentially informative both mechanistically and as a biomarker of inflammatory depression.

From cytokine buffering, the analysis then shifts toward signaling pathways that connect immune regulation with neural plasticity and tissue remodeling.

TGFBR2 is highly relevant to depression because transforming growth factor beta signaling occupies a central position at the intersection of immune regulation, neuroplasticity, extracellular matrix remodeling, and stress adaptation. Depression has been associated with altered transforming growth factor beta pathway activity in both peripheral tissues and the brain, and these changes may influence microglial behavior, neurogenesis, synaptic remodeling, and the balance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory signaling. The receptor's canonical SMAD-dependent signaling and non-canonical apoptotic pathways suggest that dysregulation could contribute to both inflammatory persistence and structural brain changes observed in mood disorders. Its role in immunosuppression is also important, as depression may involve not merely excessive inflammation but impaired regulation of inflammatory resolution. Accordingly, TGFBR2 represents a biologically plausible node linking immune dysregulation to maladaptive neural plasticity.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) [PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) 

Closely related to this broader remodeling framework, several proteins in the list may connect vascular adaptation, glial support, and developmental signaling.

CCN3 stands out because it connects developmental signaling, angiogenesis, hypoxia-related pathways, and astroglial responses, each of which has emerging relevance to depression. Altered neurovascular function and impaired glial support are increasingly recognized in depressive disorders, particularly in chronic stress states. CCN3 can negatively regulate angiogenesis while also influencing hypoxia inducible factor 1 subunit alpha-related responses, suggesting possible relevance to cerebral blood flow adaptation and metabolic stress. Importantly, its role in protective astrogenesis after injury points toward a potential contribution to glial resilience, a process closely tied to synaptic maintenance and mood regulation. Given that astrocyte dysfunction and reduced neurotrophic support are recurrent findings in depression, CCN3 may represent an underappreciated mediator linking vascular, glial, and developmental aspects of disease biology.

A more directly neurotrophic and regenerative dimension is suggested by the next candidate.

MDK is one of the most biologically interesting proteins in this dataset for depression because it spans neurodevelopmental, inflammatory, regenerative, and vascular functions. It promotes neuronal survival and migration, supports neural precursor cell growth, and modulates inflammatory-cell recruitment, placing it at the center of mechanisms that are highly relevant to stress-induced brain remodeling. Depression has been linked to impaired neuroplasticity, altered neuroimmune signaling, and vascular dysfunction; MDK could influence all three through mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling, vascular endothelial growth factor A induction, and nitric oxide-related vasodilation. Its ability to suppress tolerogenic dendritic-cell development and promote T-cell expansion further suggests a role in sustaining inflammatory states that may contribute to depressive symptoms. Thus, MDK may be particularly relevant to depression subtypes characterized by combined neuroinflammatory and neuroplasticity deficits.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

Consistent with this emphasis on trophic support, another protein in the set appears relevant to reward circuitry and dopaminergic function.

GFRA1 is especially relevant to depression because it participates in glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor and rearranged during transfection signaling, a pathway critical for dopaminergic neuron survival and function. Dopamine circuits govern motivation, reward processing, psychomotor activity, and reinforcement learning, all of which are disrupted in major depressive disorder, particularly in anhedonic presentations. By supporting dopaminergic differentiation and dopamine uptake, GFRA1 may influence mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways central to mood and motivation. Disturbance of trophic support within these circuits has been proposed as a contributor to stress susceptibility and reduced reward sensitivity, making GFRA1 a strong candidate for involvement in depression-related neuroplasticity mechanisms.

In addition to trophic signaling, vascular and metabolic regulation may also shape depressive pathophysiology.

DDAH1 is relevant because nitric oxide signaling influences vascular tone, neurovascular coupling, synaptic plasticity, and inflammatory signaling, all of which have been implicated in depression. By degrading asymmetric dimethylarginine and monomethylarginine, DDAH1 promotes nitric oxide production and may therefore affect endothelial function and cerebral perfusion. This is noteworthy because depression has been associated with endothelial dysfunction, increased cardiovascular comorbidity, and abnormalities in brain blood flow and metabolic regulation. In addition, nitric oxide can modulate neurotransmission and immune responses, suggesting that altered DDAH1 activity could contribute to both vascular and neuroimmune dimensions of depressive illness.

This vascular theme also intersects with cellular stress resilience.

HSPB6 is of interest in depression primarily through stress biology and vascular-neurotrophic mechanisms. Heat shock proteins are central components of the cellular stress response, and disturbances in proteostasis and resilience pathways may contribute to chronic stress susceptibility. HSPB6 additionally influences vasorelaxation and angiogenesis, processes relevant to the growing recognition of vascular contributions to mood disorders. Its stabilization of YWHAZ is notable because 14-3-3 family proteins participate in neurotransmitter signaling, apoptosis regulation, and synaptic plasticity. Accordingly, HSPB6 may connect systemic stress adaptation with cellular survival mechanisms that are pertinent to depression and its cardiovascular comorbidity.

A complementary perspective on stress adaptation is provided by circulating factors that signal aversive physiological states to the brain.

GDF15 is highly relevant to depression because it is a prototypical stress-responsive circulating factor that acts on discrete brainstem circuits controlling aversion, appetite, and behavioral adaptation to physiological stress. Appetite loss, malaise, fatigue, and behavioral withdrawal are prominent features of both sickness behavior and many depressive syndromes. The growth differentiation factor 15 and glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor family receptor alpha-like pathway therefore provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how peripheral stress states, including cancer, drug exposure, or metabolic stress, can induce centrally mediated aversive and anorectic behaviors that overlap with depressive symptom domains. Its activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B pathways in brainstem neurons further supports a direct neurobiological role in stress-related behavioral regulation.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

Related to this neurovegetative dimension, another candidate may reflect altered appetite and autonomic regulation.

NUCB2 is relevant to depression because appetite disturbance, altered energy balance, and autonomic dysregulation are core features of many depressive states. As an anorexigenic signal acting in hypothalamic circuits, NUCB2 may participate in the neuroendocrine control of feeding and motivational state. This is particularly important because depression frequently presents with either reduced appetite and weight loss or, in atypical forms, dysregulated energy homeostasis more broadly. Its additional effects on blood pressure and vascular resistance suggest a link to autonomic imbalance, another common biological correlate of mood disorders. NUCB2 therefore aligns well with the neurovegetative dimension of depression.

The analysis also includes proteins that may connect immune activation with cellular energetics.

TNFRSF9 is noteworthy because it links adaptive immune activation with mitochondrial function in T cells, two domains increasingly implicated in depression. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurring theme in mood-disorder biology, while altered T-cell activation and immune surveillance are also reported in subsets of depressed patients. By promoting both cluster of differentiation 8-positive T-cell survival and mitochondrial activity, TNFRSF9 may reflect an axis through which chronic immune activation influences systemic energy metabolism and inflammatory signaling. Although its role in depression is likely indirect, it may be particularly relevant in inflammation-associated depression or in depressive symptoms occurring in the context of chronic infection, cancer, or immunotherapy.

From immune energetics, attention then turns to intracellular quality-control pathways that may influence stress resilience.

LAMP3 is relevant to depression because autophagy, lysosomal function, and proteostasis are increasingly recognized as important determinants of neuronal resilience under chronic stress. Impaired autophagic flux and endolysosomal dysfunction can affect synaptic turnover, neuroinflammation, and cell survival, all of which are implicated in depressive pathology. LAMP3 also participates in dendritic-cell biology, raising the possibility that it influences both neural and immune components of disease. Given the growing interest in cellular quality-control pathways in stress-related psychiatric disorders, LAMP3 represents a plausible contributor to depression through mechanisms involving impaired stress adaptation and inflammatory signaling.

A similarly broad integrative role may be considered for transcriptional regulators that respond to mechanical and growth-related signals.

Although the functional annotation provided here is brief, YAP1 stands out because erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 signaling has recognized importance in neurodevelopment, synaptic regulation, and cortical circuit function. YAP1 is a major effector of Hippo signaling and broadly regulates cell survival, proliferation, and mechanotransduction; its ability to activate erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 fragments suggests potential relevance to neuronal plasticity and stress-responsive transcriptional programs. Since depression is strongly associated with impaired synaptic remodeling and altered growth-factor signaling, YAP1 may represent a convergence point between cellular stress sensing and neurotrophic regulation. This makes it a potentially important, if indirect, candidate in depression biology.

Another mechanistic intersection emerges in proteins that link innate immune sensing with mitochondrial homeostasis.

RNASET2 is particularly interesting because it connects innate immune sensing with mitochondrial ribonucleic acid metabolism. Both toll-like receptor-mediated inflammatory activation and mitochondrial dysfunction are central themes in current models of depression. By generating ribonucleic acid degradation products that stimulate toll-like receptor 8 and toll-like receptor 7, RNASET2 may amplify antiviral and inflammatory signaling pathways that can influence mood through cytokine-mediated effects on the brain. Its additional role in mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover is equally important, as mitochondrial stress can trigger inflammation and impair cellular energetics, both of which are implicated in depressive disorders. RNASET2 therefore sits at a mechanistic intersection highly relevant to neuroimmune models of depression.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

The final proteins in the list further reinforce the possible contribution of endothelial and angiogenic regulation.

ACVRL1 is relevant because it links transforming growth factor beta family signaling to endothelial biology and angiogenic restraint. Vascular dysfunction and impaired neurovascular coupling have been increasingly associated with depression, particularly in late-life depression and in individuals with inflammatory or metabolic comorbidity. Through SMAD1-dependent endothelial signaling, ACVRL1 may influence microvascular remodeling and tissue perfusion, including potentially within the brain. Given the broader importance of transforming growth factor beta superfamily pathways in stress adaptation and inflammation, ACVRL1 may contribute to depression through cerebrovascular and endothelial mechanisms rather than direct neuronal effects.

In a closely related manner, anti-angiogenic regulation may also shape neural plasticity-relevant vascular support.

COL18A1 is noteworthy because anti-angiogenic signaling may influence brain vascular plasticity and neurotrophic support, both of which are relevant to depression. Vascular endothelial growth factor-related pathways have repeatedly been implicated in antidepressant responses, stress resilience, and hippocampal plasticity. A molecule that suppresses vascular endothelial growth factor A and kinase insert domain receptor signaling could therefore modulate the same biological systems that support neurogenesis and adaptive vascular remodeling. While the relationship is likely context-dependent, COL18A1 may be important in depression through its capacity to restrain angiogenic and vascular endothelial growth factor-mediated processes that are often considered beneficial for mood-related neural plasticity.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123)

### Factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (TF:M10023_1) 

The pathway described here centers on the transcription factor tumor protein fifty three and its recognition of a canonical deoxyribonucleic acid response element represented by the motif NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. Tumor protein fifty three is a sequence specific transcriptional regulator that is activated by diverse forms of cellular stress, including deoxyribonucleic acid damage, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, metabolic disturbance, and excitotoxic injury. After activation, tumor protein fifty three binds to response elements in chromatin and regulates a broad gene network controlling cell cycle arrest, deoxyribonucleic acid repair, senescence, apoptosis, autophagy, redox balance, and mitochondrial homeostasis. Because these processes are central to neuronal survival and plasticity, tumor protein fifty three signaling is highly relevant to brain function. In the nervous system, excessive or persistent tumor protein fifty three activity can promote neuronal atrophy or cell death, impair synaptic maintenance, and intensify neuroinflammatory and oxidative injury, whereas balanced tumor protein fifty three signaling may contribute to adaptive stress responses and genome protection. Thus, a pathway defined by tumor protein fifty three motif occupancy should be understood as a stress responsive transcriptional program that links environmental and intracellular insults to long term changes in cellular viability and tissue integrity, including in brain regions implicated in mood regulation.

With this biological framework in mind, the possible relationship between this stress responsive program and depression can be considered cautiously on mechanistic grounds.

No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a literature supported pathway to depression cannot be established from the supplied citation set alone. Nevertheless, from a biological standpoint, the tumor protein fifty three pathway is plausibly related to depression because several mechanisms commonly implicated in depression converge on cellular stress programs that are regulated by tumor protein fifty three. Depression has been associated in many studies with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired neuroplasticity, and in some contexts increased neuronal vulnerability in corticolimbic circuits. Tumor protein fifty three is a master regulator of exactly these stress response domains: it can be activated by oxidative and inflammatory injury, alter mitochondrial function and cellular metabolism, and induce transcriptional programs leading to apoptosis, senescence, or reduced cellular resilience. In brain tissue, sustained activation of such a program could theoretically contribute to synaptic loss, reduced structural plasticity, and impaired survival of stress sensitive neurons or glial cells, all of which are processes relevant to depressive pathophysiology. Conversely, modulation of tumor protein fifty three dependent transcription might influence stress adaptation and the balance between damage containment and tissue preservation. However, because the publication list is empty, these connections should be regarded as mechanistic inference rather than conclusions directly supported by the provided references.

This cautious interpretation is further informed by the enrichment results, which provide a quantitative basis for considering whether depression associated molecular changes may converge on this regulatory axis.

There were 17 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in a tumor protein fifty three centered stress responsive transcriptional pathway defined by recognition of the canonical deoxyribonucleic acid response element NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. This enrichment indicates that the analyzed protein set converges on a regulatory program that links cellular stress sensing to transcriptional control of cell cycle arrest, deoxyribonucleic acid repair, senescence, apoptosis, autophagy, redox balance, and mitochondrial homeostasis. Given that this pathway integrates multiple stress inputs, including deoxyribonucleic acid damage, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, metabolic disturbance, and excitotoxic injury, the presence of 17 enriched proteins supports a quantitatively substantial connection between depression-associated molecular alterations and tumor protein fifty three dependent control of neuronal survival, synaptic maintenance, and tissue integrity in brain regions involved in mood regulation. We will introduce these proteins in detail in the following.

Consistent with this network level view, the functional enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be biologically relevant and are therefore discussed below in greater detail.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, GDF15 stands out as the most directly relevant to depression because it links systemic stress signaling to central neural circuits that regulate appetite, aversion, energy balance, and sickness behavior. These domains are highly pertinent to depressive symptomatology, particularly reduced appetite, weight loss, fatigue, motivational suppression, and the broader syndrome of inflammation- or illness-associated depression. The described GDF15-GFRAL pathway is activated by diverse stressors, including anticancer drugs, cancer, and metformin, and engages brainstem neurons in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius, regions that influence visceral sensation and behavioral avoidance. Such stress-responsive aversive signaling may contribute to anhedonia-like or malaise-related behavioral states that overlap with depressive phenotypes. Its coupling to RET autophosphorylation and MAPK/AKT pathways further suggests potential integration with neuroplasticity and stress-adaptation mechanisms that are frequently implicated in mood disorders. Therefore, although GDF15 is not a canonical depression gene, its role in coordinating stress-induced aversion, appetite suppression, and metabolic adaptation makes it especially notable in the context of depression, particularly depression accompanied by somatic and inflammatory features.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

From this stress signaling example, the discussion naturally extends to proteins that may connect depression associated biology with immune activation and inflammatory regulation.

IFNL1 is relevant to depression because immune activation and interferon-related signaling are strongly implicated in the pathophysiology of mood disorders, especially inflammation-associated depression. The receptor complex activates the JAK/STAT pathway and induces interferon-stimulated genes, placing this protein within a molecular framework that connects peripheral immune signals to sustained transcriptional changes. Interferon signaling has long been associated with depressive symptoms in clinical settings, and cytokine-driven behavioral changes such as fatigue, social withdrawal, and anhedonia are considered mechanistically important in subsets of depression. Although the description here emphasizes antiviral defense rather than direct neuropsychiatric effects, the broader biology of interferon pathways makes IFNL1 a noteworthy candidate for relevance to depression, particularly where immune dysregulation, chronic infection, or inflammatory stress contribute to disease expression.

A related immune linked mechanism is suggested by IFI30, which may be relevant through antigen processing and neuroinflammatory pathways.

IFI30 is potentially relevant to depression through the increasingly recognized interface between immune activation, antigen presentation, and neuroinflammation. By promoting antigen processing and both MHC class II presentation and cross-presentation, IFI30 contributes to adaptive immune activation and the shaping of inflammatory responses. This is important because depression in many patients is associated with altered immune tone, increased inflammatory mediators, and evidence of aberrant crosstalk between peripheral immunity and the brain. While IFI30 is not specifically a neuronal protein, its function in lysosomal redox processing and antigen presentation suggests a plausible role in inflammatory states that may secondarily affect mood, motivation, and cognition. Thus, IFI30 is best viewed as an indirect but biologically credible link to depression through immune-mediated disease mechanisms.

Moving from immune regulation to neuronal gene control, RBFOX3 may be of interest because it points toward post-transcriptional processes that influence circuit stability.

RBFOX3 is of interest because RNA splicing regulation is fundamental to neuronal identity, synaptic function, and circuit stability, all of which are central to depression biology. Although the provided annotation focuses specifically on regulation of RBFOX2 splicing and nonsense-mediated decay, the RBFOX family is widely associated with neuronal transcriptome control. Disturbances in alternative splicing can alter excitability, neurotransmission, and synaptic plasticity, which are major mechanistic themes in mood disorders. In this context, RBFOX3 may be relevant not because it directly mediates depressive symptoms, but because it participates in post-transcriptional regulatory networks that could influence neuronal resilience or vulnerability under stress. Its strongest relevance is therefore likely to lie in neurodevelopmental and circuit-level mechanisms that intersect with depression risk.

Another indirect but conceptually related candidate is EDA2R, which converges on signaling pathways often discussed in the context of cellular stress and inflammatory adaptation.

EDA2R merits attention because it signals through NF-kappa-B and JNK, two pathways that are broadly involved in inflammation, cellular stress responses, and apoptosis-related processes. These pathways have been repeatedly implicated in depression, especially in models emphasizing chronic stress, inflammatory activation, and impaired neuroplasticity. Although EDA2R is not classically associated with psychiatric disease, receptors that converge on TRAF-dependent NF-kappa-B/JNK signaling may influence how cells respond to stressors at both peripheral and potentially central levels. Its relevance to depression is therefore indirect but conceptually meaningful, particularly in relation to inflammatory signaling cascades that can modulate brain function and behavior.

In addition to inflammatory signaling, several proteins in the enriched set point toward peripheral barrier systems and gut related processes that may intersect with depression associated biology.

TFF3 is notable because it points to the gut-brain axis, an area of increasing importance in depression research. By supporting intestinal mucosal maintenance and repair, TFF3 may help preserve epithelial barrier integrity and limit gut-derived inflammatory signaling. This is relevant because intestinal barrier dysfunction, altered microbiota-host interactions, and low-grade systemic inflammation have all been linked to depressive symptoms in at least a subset of patients. A protein involved in mucosal healing may therefore influence depression indirectly by modulating gastrointestinal homeostasis and immune activation. While the annotation does not describe direct neurobiological effects, TFF3 is still a meaningful candidate in the context of somatic-inflammatory mechanisms contributing to depression.

Closely aligned with this barrier centered perspective, PIGR may also be relevant through its role in mucosal immune homeostasis.

PIGR may have relevance to depression through mucosal immunity and the gut-brain axis. Secretory IgA is a key mediator of mucosal immune defense, and proteins that regulate IgA handling can influence host-microbiome interactions, epithelial barrier function, and inflammatory tone. These processes are increasingly implicated in depression, especially where gastrointestinal symptoms, immune dysregulation, or microbiome alterations are present. Although PIGR is not directly linked to neural signaling, its role in mucosal immune homeostasis makes it a plausible indirect contributor to depression-related biology via peripheral immune and barrier mechanisms.

Finally, the enriched set also includes a protein linked to oxidative balance, thereby returning the discussion to one of the central stress response themes introduced at the outset.

GGT1 is potentially relevant to depression because it participates in glutathione metabolism and therefore in the regulation of oxidative stress, a process frequently implicated in depressive disorders. Glutathione is a major antioxidant, and disturbances in redox balance have been associated with neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired neuronal resilience in depression. In addition, GGT1 contributes to leukotriene metabolism, linking it to inflammatory signaling. Although the annotation emphasizes extracellular glutathione turnover and skeletal biology rather than brain-specific effects, the combined relevance to oxidative and inflammatory homeostasis makes GGT1 biologically interesting in the context of depression, particularly for systemic mechanisms that may influence brain function.[PubMed:12810527](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12810527)

### Abnormal pleura morphology (HP:0002103) 

Abnormal pleura morphology refers to structural alterations of the pulmonary pleura, the mesothelial membrane that envelops the lungs and lines the thoracic cavity. Although this pathway is anatomically centered in the thorax rather than the brain, the pleura is biologically integrated with systemic immune signaling, vascular permeability, inflammatory cytokine production, and tissue remodeling. These processes are highly relevant to depression because depression is increasingly understood as a multisystem disorder involving peripheral inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, neuroimmune communication, and altered organ morphology beyond the central nervous system. In the context of pleural abnormality, morphological disruption may reflect or contribute to chronic inflammatory states, altered barrier properties, and dysregulated immune cell trafficking, all of which could influence brain function indirectly through circulating mediators. 

Viewed in this broader framework, the available literature does not directly examine pleural structure in depression, but it does consistently indicate that depression is associated with abnormal morphology in multiple tissues and cellular compartments, including cerebral blood vessels, gray matter, dendritic spines, hippocampal neurons, amygdalar neurons, mitochondria, testis, spleen, and other peripheral organs. This pattern supports the interpretation that abnormal pleura morphology, if present in depressed individuals or depression models, would most plausibly participate in disease biology through systemic inflammatory and vascular pathways rather than through a pleura-specific mechanism.

This general interpretation is further supported by the studies provided below. The literature supports an indirect but biologically plausible relationship between abnormal pleura morphology and depression through shared mechanisms of inflammation, vascular pathology, and systemic organ remodeling. The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from work showing that chronic social stress induces vascular structural abnormalities together with loss of endothelial tight junction integrity, enabling peripheral interleukin six to enter the brain and promote depression-like behaviors; this study directly links peripheral inflammatory signaling, vascular morphology, and depressive phenotypes, thereby providing a framework by which structural abnormalities in non-neural barrier tissues could also contribute to depression if they amplify systemic cytokine exposure or endothelial dysfunction (PubMed:29184215). This interpretation is reinforced by reviews of late-life depression that describe depression as a brain network dysfunction disorder shaped not only by neurotransmitter abnormalities but also by neuroinflammation, neuroimmune dysregulation, oxidative stress, and cerebrovascular processes (PubMed:37145167). Across the remaining studies, depression is repeatedly associated with abnormal morphology at multiple biological scales, including altered gray matter volume and structural covariance in the basal ganglia-limbic system (PubMed:41356243), shallower olfactory sulci as a possible trait marker of vulnerability (PubMed:27526191), altered cortical surface morphology in suicidal depression (PubMed:38665310), distinct structural abnormalities in anxious depression (PubMed:40787685), and age-at-onset-specific gray matter changes (PubMed:41577042). Experimental models further show neuronal and subcellular morphological injury in depression-related states, such as hippocampal neuronal damage associated with inflammatory signaling (PubMed:37634821), amygdalar dendritic spine remodeling after severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two infection with depression-like behavior (PubMed:40365287), mitochondrial morphological abnormalities linked to depressive pathogenesis (PubMed:38678964), and testicular morphological injury in chronic stress-induced depression (PubMed:38244803). Importantly, depression has also been associated with enlarged spleen volume and altered immune markers, indicating that peripheral organ morphology can track immune dysregulation relevant to depressive illness (PubMed:40355817). Taken together, these studies suggest that abnormal pleura morphology is unlikely to represent a core canonical lesion of depression, but it may be relevant as a peripheral manifestation or contributor within the broader depression-associated network of inflammatory activation, endothelial-barrier disruption, and multisystem morphological remodeling that can influence brain function and depressive symptom expression.[PubMed:29184215](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29184215) [PubMed:37145167](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37145167) [PubMed:41356243](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41356243) [PubMed:27526191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27526191) [PubMed:38665310](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38665310) [PubMed:40787685](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40787685) [PubMed:41577042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41577042) [PubMed:37634821](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37634821) [PubMed:40365287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40365287) [PubMed:38678964](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38678964) [PubMed:38244803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38244803) [PubMed:40355817](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40355817) 

Consistent with this systems-level interpretation, the enrichment results also point toward a potentially relevant connection. There were 10 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of abnormal pleura morphology. This enrichment links a thoracic structural phenotype to depression through quantitatively relevant systemic processes, because the pleura participates in immune signaling, vascular permeability, cytokine production, and tissue remodeling, all of which are repeatedly implicated in depression as a multisystem disorder rather than a condition restricted to the brain. Although the present pathway is anatomically localized to the pulmonary pleura, the biological interpretation is strengthened by convergent evidence that depression is associated with abnormal morphology across multiple tissues and subcellular compartments, including cerebral blood vessels, gray matter, dendritic spines, hippocampal neurons, amygdalar neurons, mitochondria, testis, and spleen. In this context, the identification of 10 proteins supports a model in which pleural morphological alteration, if present, would most plausibly reflect broader inflammatory, endothelial, and neuroimmune dysregulation that contributes to depression biology through circulating mediators and altered tissue barrier properties rather than through an isolated pleural mechanism.

Building on this network-level overview, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, EPHB4 stands out as one of the most plausibly relevant to depression because its core functions converge on vascular biology, cell-cell signaling, and tissue remodeling. Depression is increasingly understood not only as a neurotransmitter-associated disorder but also as a condition involving neurovascular dysfunction, altered blood-brain barrier integrity, inflammatory signaling, and impaired structural plasticity. A receptor that governs angiogenesis, vascular remodeling, and permeability may therefore be mechanistically relevant to depressive pathophysiology, particularly in the context of cerebrovascular dysfunction and stress-related changes in the neurovascular unit. In addition, the ephrin-Eph signaling system is broadly implicated in cell positioning, migration, and intercellular communication, processes that are also important for neural circuit organization and adaptive plasticity. Although the provided annotation does not directly describe neuronal functions, the vascular and adhesion-related roles of EPHB4 make it a strong candidate for indirect involvement in depression through altered cerebral perfusion, endothelial signaling, and neuroinflammatory coupling.

A related but distinct line of reasoning applies to ELN, which may connect extracellular matrix biology with vascular integrity in depression-relevant contexts. ELN is highly relevant because it links extracellular matrix biology to vascular integrity and angiotensin-associated signaling, both of which have meaningful connections to depression. A growing body of evidence suggests that depression is associated with systemic vascular dysfunction, increased arterial stiffness, inflammatory remodeling, and dysregulation of stress-responsive cardiovascular pathways. ELN is a structural determinant of vessel elasticity and wall integrity, and its involvement in smooth muscle maturation, collagen-elastin cross-linking, and angiotensin-related control of vascular smooth muscle proliferation makes it especially noteworthy. These functions suggest that ELN may contribute to the vascular component of depression, particularly in patients with comorbid cardiovascular disease, chronic stress exposure, or impaired cerebral blood flow regulation. Its extracellular matrix remodeling role is also potentially relevant because matrix composition influences cellular signaling, inflammation, and tissue resilience, all of which may shape susceptibility to chronic stress and depressive illness.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

Shifting from vascular and extracellular matrix processes to epithelial barrier biology, AGR2 raises a different but still potentially relevant mechanism. AGR2 is notable primarily because of its role in MUC2 synthesis and mucus biology, which may connect to depression through the gut-brain axis. There is substantial interest in the contribution of intestinal barrier integrity, mucosal immune signaling, and microbiome-host interactions to depressive symptoms. A protein required for proper mucus production could influence epithelial protection, microbial composition, and inflammatory tone, thereby affecting systemic and neural pathways implicated in depression. Its additional functions in cell adhesion, migration, differentiation, and growth further suggest a broader role in epithelial homeostasis and stress responses. Although the evidence provided here does not directly place AGR2 in neuropsychiatric pathways, its involvement in intestinal mucosal function makes it an interesting candidate for indirect relevance to depression, especially in inflammation-associated or gut-mediated disease mechanisms.[PubMed:23274113](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23274113) 

By comparison, the connection of SPINK1 to depression appears more limited and should be interpreted more cautiously. SPINK1 appears less directly connected to depression than EPHB4, ELN, or AGR2. However, its annotation includes modulation of calcium uptake and nitric oxide production, two signaling processes that are broadly relevant to neural function, synaptic plasticity, and stress biology. Nitric oxide signaling has been implicated in mood regulation, neuroinflammation, and antidepressant response, while calcium homeostasis is fundamental to neuronal excitability and intracellular signaling. Nonetheless, the specific function provided here is restricted to sperm physiology in the male reproductive tract, which limits the strength of any direct inference for depression. Therefore, SPINK1 should be considered only a speculative and relatively low-priority candidate based on the current functional annotation.[PubMed:14645103](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14645103) [PubMed:16083722](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16083722) [PubMed:22228629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22228629) [PubMed:9828198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9828198) 

Finally, SCARB2 appears to have the weakest direct connection within the present set of annotations. SCARB2 is the least directly informative candidate in relation to depression based on the annotation provided. Its listed function concerns viral entry, specifically as a receptor for enterovirus 71. While infection, immune activation, and neuroinflammatory responses can influence depressive symptoms, the present functional description does not provide a sufficiently strong mechanistic bridge to depression compared with the vascular, extracellular matrix, and gut-barrier related proteins above. SCARB2 may still be relevant in broader infection-associated neuropsychiatric contexts, but the current evidence is limited and indirect.

### Bone pain (HP:0002653) 

Bone pain is an unpleasant sensory and affective experience localized to osseous tissue and commonly described as aching, throbbing, stabbing, or deep persistent discomfort. It arises in diverse clinical settings, including degenerative spine disease, cancer involving bone, chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder, osteoporosis, fracture repair, and rare skeletal disorders. Although it is experienced at the level of the skeleton, bone pain is not a purely local phenomenon. Rather, it may reflect the integration of peripheral nociceptive signaling from bone marrow, periosteum, trabecular microdamage, inflammatory mediators, osteoclast activity, mechanical instability, and neural sensitization with central processing in brain regions that regulate affect, motivation, and stress responses. The publications provided further suggest that bone pain is closely linked to impaired quality of life, reduced physical function, sleep disturbance, psychological distress, and depressive symptoms. In addition, emerging evidence indicates that bone related inflammatory and immune processes may intersect with neuroimmune pathways relevant to depression, including skull bone marrow inflammatory signaling, microglial activation, and stress responsive catecholaminergic mechanisms. Taken together, bone pain may be more appropriately understood as a multidimensional pathway connecting skeletal pathology, inflammation, stress biology, functional disability, and mood disturbance rather than as an isolated somatic symptom.

Building on this conceptual framework, the collected literature supports a strong and biologically plausible relationship between bone pain and depression through both clinical and mechanistic pathways. Clinically, studies of skeletal and orthopedic disease consistently show that greater pain burden is associated with higher depressive symptom severity, worse function, and poorer quality of life. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, bone pain was highly prevalent and showed a significant positive correlation with depression scores, while quality of life partly mediated this relationship, suggesting that persistent skeletal pain may contribute to depression both directly and indirectly through disability and restriction of daily activities. Similar patterns were reported in patients with chronic kidney disease receiving hemodialysis, in whom bone alterations and pain were accompanied by worse physical functioning and higher anxiety and depression scores. In degenerative cervical and lumbar spine disease, depression was common among patients with greater neck or back pain and worse disability, and although depressed patients improved after surgery, they remained more symptomatic both before and after intervention, suggesting a durable reciprocal relationship between pain and mood. Related orthopedic literature further indicates that pain catastrophizing, anxiety, and depression cluster with painful hip pathology, reinforcing the view that chronic musculoskeletal pain states may amplify depressive burden. Beyond these clinical associations, several publications point to shared mechanisms. A neuroimmune imaging study in depression identified inflammatory activity in skull bone marrow and adjacent meningeal regions that correlated with both peripheral cytokines and central inflammatory signals, raising the possibility that bone associated immune compartments may participate in pathways relevant to depressive pathophysiology. Experimental work on cancer induced bone pain demonstrated comorbid depressive like states accompanied by inflammatory and immune changes in the hippocampus and amygdala, including major histocompatibility complex class one related microglial signaling and enrichment of nuclear factor kappa light chain enhancer of activated B cells and T helper seventeen cell pathways, suggesting that persistent bone pain can engage central immune circuits implicated in depression. Additional translational evidence shows that psychological stress and depression are associated with impaired bone healing and altered local catecholamine signaling in bone, supporting bidirectional communication in which depression related stress biology may worsen skeletal pathology and potentially sustain pain. The therapeutic overlap is also notable, as perioperative ketamine reduced both postoperative pain and depressive symptoms, implying at least partial convergence of pain and mood regulatory systems. Overall, the available evidence indicates that bone pain is related to depression through an interconnected network involving chronic nociceptive input, inflammation, neuroimmune activation, stress signaling, reduced mobility, and diminished quality of life, making bone pain both a correlate of and a potential contributor to depressive illness.[PubMed:38277149](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38277149) [PubMed:36670198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36670198) [PubMed:39657983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39657983) [PubMed:37277336](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37277336) [PubMed:30266081](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30266081) [PubMed:31256659](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31256659) [PubMed:36684946](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36684946) [PubMed:34440578](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34440578) [PubMed:29855190](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29855190) [PubMed:39554478](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39554478) [PubMed:33165035](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33165035) [PubMed:34730463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34730463) [PubMed:39727925](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39727925) 

Consistent with this literature based interpretation, the enrichment analysis also identified a compact set of depression associated proteins linked to this functional theme. There were 9 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing bone pain as a multidimensional sensory, inflammatory, and affective process that links skeletal pathology with stress biology, functional impairment, and mood disturbance. This enrichment is consistent with the clinical observation that bone pain is not restricted to local osseous injury but instead reflects the convergence of peripheral nociceptive input, inflammatory signaling, neural sensitization, and central affective processing, all of which are highly relevant to depression. The inclusion of 9 proteins in this function enrichment analysis suggests a focused but biologically meaningful network connecting bone related inflammatory activity, pain related signaling, and depression associated neuroimmune and behavioral mechanisms.

With this network context in place, the following section introduces the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance in a more detailed and sequential manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, TREM2 is the most directly relevant to depression because it is centrally involved in microglial biology, neuroinflammation, and neuron-glia interactions. Depression is increasingly understood to involve immune dysregulation and inflammatory signaling within the central nervous system, and microglia are key mediators of these processes. The reported requirement of TREM2-TYROBP signaling for phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons and for control of microglial superoxide production indicates a role in synaptic and neuronal homeostasis, processes that are highly pertinent to stress-related neural remodeling and depressive symptomatology. Moreover, the observation that this pathway promotes pro-inflammatory microglial responses after nerve injury suggests a plausible mechanistic link to inflammation-associated depression, in which activated innate immune pathways contribute to neuronal dysfunction and behavioral changes. Its additional effects on IL10 production and dendritic-cell immunoregulation further support the view that TREM2 participates in balancing inflammatory versus anti-inflammatory responses, a theme strongly implicated in depression pathophysiology.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

Moving from a primarily microglia centered candidate to a broader regulator of tissue signaling, TGFB1 also appears noteworthy in this context. TGFB1 stands out because transforming growth factor-beta signaling is broadly involved in immune regulation, tissue remodeling, apoptosis, and neuroplasticity, all of which are relevant to depression. Although the specific function provided here concerns promotion of cell death during mammary gland involution, the underlying biology points to a potent role in apoptotic signaling and tissue homeostasis. In the context of depression, TGFB-family pathways are of interest because excessive or dysregulated apoptotic and inflammatory signaling can impair neuronal resilience, alter synaptic connectivity, and contribute to stress-induced brain changes. Thus, even though the annotation is not brain-specific, TGFB1 remains noteworthy as a signaling molecule with plausible relevance to depression through its broader roles in inflammatory control and cell survival-death balance.

A related but somewhat more systemic line of reasoning applies to FGF23, which may connect bone associated biology with aging and metabolic pathways relevant to brain function. FGF23 is potentially relevant to depression because the annotation connects it to Klotho biology and modulation of insulin/IGF1 signaling, pathways increasingly associated with aging, metabolic dysfunction, and brain health. Depression frequently co-occurs with accelerated biological aging and metabolic abnormalities, and insulin/IGF1 signaling has been implicated in neuroplasticity, stress responsiveness, and cognitive dysfunction. Klotho itself has attracted attention for neuroprotective and anti-aging properties, raising the possibility that dysregulation of this axis could influence vulnerability to depressive symptoms, particularly in aging or medically ill populations. Although the evidence in the provided annotation is indirect and not depression-specific, FGF23 is notable because it intersects with systemic pathways that can shape central nervous system resilience.

In a similar vein, PSAP appears relevant through molecular processes that influence transcriptional regulation and cellular survival. PSAP is of interest because it links epigenetic repression, messenger ribonucleic acid splicing, and apoptosis regulation, all of which are biologically plausible contributors to depression. The involvement of PSAP in SIN3-HDAC1-mediated transcriptional repression suggests a connection to chromatin remodeling, a mechanism widely implicated in stress responses and antidepressant action. Its role in the splicing modulation of BCL2L1/Bcl-X is particularly relevant, since altered balance between pro-survival and pro-apoptotic signaling may influence neuronal integrity and stress susceptibility. In depression, disrupted ribonucleic acid processing and maladaptive transcriptional programs have been reported in both neurons and glial cells; therefore, a factor that coordinates repression and apoptotic splice choice could contribute to disease mechanisms involving impaired cellular resilience. While the annotation does not provide direct psychiatric evidence, PSAP stands out as a mechanistically rich candidate with potential relevance to depression-related molecular pathology.

Finally, SCARB2 appears less directly connected to depression than TREM2, TGFB1, FGF23, or PSAP, but it may still be relevant within a broader neuroimmune framework. SCARB2 appears less directly connected to depression than TREM2, TGFB1, FGF23, or PSAP, but it may still be relevant in a broader neuroimmune context. Its role as a viral receptor suggests potential involvement in host-pathogen interactions and infection-triggered inflammatory responses. Since infectious and post-infectious immune activation can precipitate neuroinflammation and depressive symptoms in some individuals, proteins that mediate microbial entry or host response may have indirect importance. However, based on the functional information provided here, SCARB2 has a comparatively limited and less specific connection to depression mechanisms.

### carbohydrate binding (GO:0030246) 

Carbohydrate binding is a molecular function in which a protein selectively and non-covalently recognizes carbohydrate structures, including simple sugars, complex oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified sugar derivatives. This function is biologically important because carbohydrates are major components of the cell surface and extracellular environment, where they regulate cell adhesion, receptor activation, immune recognition, trafficking, and intercellular communication. Proteins with carbohydrate-binding capacity include lectins, lipopolysaccharide-binding proteins, glycan-recognizing receptors, extracellular matrix-associated proteins, and signaling regulators that respond to glycolipids or glycoproteins. In the nervous system, carbohydrate-dependent interactions influence synapse formation, neuronal morphology, glial activation, blood-brain and gut-barrier signaling, and inflammatory communication between peripheral tissues and the brain. Because depression is increasingly understood as a disorder involving not only neurotransmitter imbalance but also neuroinflammation, stress-axis dysregulation, synaptic dysfunction, and altered gut-brain communication, carbohydrate-binding proteins and carbohydrate-responsive signaling systems are plausible mechanistic contributors. The pathway is therefore best viewed not as a single linear cascade, but as a functional category that links sugar-containing ligands or glycoconjugates to immune, metabolic, and neural processes relevant to depressive pathophysiology. 

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that carbohydrate binding may be related to depression through three convergent themes: immune-inflammatory signaling, gut-liver-brain communication, and more direct carbohydrate-derived regulation of neural function. A large plasma proteomics study found that proteins associated with depression were significantly enriched in carbohydrate binding together with phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, and cytokine-receptor interaction pathways, indicating that carbohydrate-binding proteins are embedded within the inflammatory molecular architecture of depression rather than acting only as isolated markers (PubMed:41500316). This interpretation is further supported by studies centered on lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, a protein that recognizes a carbohydrate-rich bacterial cell wall component and may link intestinal barrier disturbance to systemic inflammation. In individuals undergoing carbohydrate malabsorption testing, interleukin six was positively associated with depressive symptoms and with altered tryptophan-to-kynurenine metabolism, while lipopolysaccharide-binding protein correlated with the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, supporting a model in which carbohydrate-related gut dysfunction may promote inflammatory and metabolic changes relevant to depression (PubMed:33312105). Although one cross-sectional study in obstructive sleep apnea did not detect a direct association between lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and depressive symptom severity, it still linked lipopolysaccharide-binding protein to systemic inflammatory status, suggesting context dependence rather than absence of biological relevance (PubMed:40101844). A recent review of intestinal permeability biomarkers further supports the possibility that carbohydrate-recognizing innate immune mediators may help define an inflammation-related subtype of depression, even if clinical standardization remains incomplete (PubMed:41155365). Mechanistic support also comes from an animal study showing that *Bupleurum chinense* reduced hepatic lipopolysaccharide-binding protein expression, suppressed nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, restored monoamine biosynthesis, and improved depression-like behavior, thereby connecting a carbohydrate-binding inflammatory mediator to depressive phenotypes through the liver-brain axis (PubMed:41794258). Beyond peripheral inflammation, carbohydrate-derived molecules may also act more directly within the brain: glucosylceramide, a glucose-containing sphingolipid, was shown to bind and activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma in dopamine receptor D2-expressing medium spiny neurons of the dorsal striatum, and disruption of its synthesis caused depression-like behavior, whereas glucosylceramide administration reversed stress-induced depressive phenotypes (PubMed:41510157). In addition, polysaccharides from *Corydalis yanhusuo* alleviated chronic stress-induced depression-like behavior by reducing hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis overactivation, suppressing microglial activation, limiting harmful astrocyte transformation, and preserving hippocampal synaptic integrity, indicating that complex carbohydrates may modulate neuroimmune processes central to depression (PubMed:40513699). Although not a carbohydrate-binding study per se, the demonstration that hippocampal and neocortical deletion of astrocyte elevated gene-1 causes depressive behavior together with impaired dendritic structure and excitatory synaptic transmission is consistent with the broader view that pathways influencing extracellular recognition and neural morphology, including glycan-related interactions, may be relevant to depressive disease biology (PubMed:40122859). Overall, the available evidence suggests that carbohydrate binding may be related to depression because carbohydrate-recognizing proteins and carbohydrate-derived ligands participate in inflammatory sensing, barrier dysfunction, tryptophan metabolism, monoamine regulation, stress signaling, glial reactivity, and neuronal plasticity, all of which are established components of depressive pathogenesis.[PubMed:41500316](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41500316) [PubMed:33312105](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33312105) [PubMed:40101844](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40101844) [PubMed:41155365](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41155365) [PubMed:41794258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41794258) [PubMed:41510157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41510157) [PubMed:40513699](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40513699) [PubMed:40122859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40122859) 

Consistent with this broader literature context, there were 11 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the molecular function category of carbohydrate binding, a function defined by the selective and non-covalent recognition of carbohydrate structures ranging from simple sugars to complex oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and chemically modified glycan derivatives. This enrichment is biologically notable because carbohydrate-dependent recognition operates at the interface of cell surfaces and the extracellular environment, where it influences several processes that are highly relevant to depression, including immune recognition, receptor activation, cell adhesion, intercellular communication, trafficking, synapse formation, glial responses, barrier signaling, and gut-brain communication. In the context of depression, the identification of 11 proteins in this functionally coherent category supports a mechanistic framework in which glycan-sensitive proteins may connect neuroinflammation, stress-related signaling disruption, synaptic dysfunction, and peripheral-to-central immune communication, thereby extending the interpretation of depression beyond neurotransmitter-centered models toward a broader systems-level pathology.

To further contextualize these 11 proteins, the figure below illustrates their protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/df893cca-0300-49b9-b8df-d347c044deb1.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=565C1ED811DA8975)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We introduce them in detail below, moving from proteins with more direct immune-inflammatory relevance to those whose connections to depression may be more indirect or context-dependent.

CLEC4D is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to depression because it sits at the intersection of innate immune sensing, inflammatory signal amplification, and adaptive immune polarization.
